newsitem.title: USA: Judge considers Kaczynski challenge to cabin search.
newsitem.headline: Judge considers Kaczynski challenge to cabin search.

text.p: Attorneys for Unabomber suspect Theodore Kaczynski urged a federal judge Friday to throw out critical evidence seized from his remote Montana cabin.
The defence also told the court it did not plan to ask for the highly-publicised case to be moved from Sacramento, where Kaczynski is due to go on trial in November.
Kaczynski, a former mathematics professor, is accused of being the shadowy Unabomber, who killed three people and injured 23 during an anti-technology bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995.
He was arrested in Montana a year ago and has pleaded not guilty to charges accusing him of four bomb attacks in Sacramento, two of them fatal.
Last week, federal prosecutors said they would seek the death penalty if he were convicted.
"We would like to try it here if we can," lead defence attorney Quin Denvir told U.S. District Judge Garland Burrell, the judge in charge of the case.
Some observers thought the defence would seek a change of venue because of pretrial publicity in Sacramento.
The defence team on Friday urged Burrell to throw out all of the evidence seized by the FBI at the cabin.
The defence alleged the search was illegal because the FBI's affidavit supporting its request for a search warrant contained misleading information.

Denvir said the FBI had "no solid evidence," only the "illusion of evidence" against Kaczynski when it sought the search warrant. He accused the government of making "grave misrepresentations" to the judge who granted the warrant.
Denvir called for a special court hearing to determine if federal investigators applied undo pressure to gain access to the cabin.
The evidence from the cabin is crucial to the government's case.

Investigators found handwritten and handprinted documents at Kaczynski's cabin, written in English, Spanish and numeric code, according to court documents. Prosecutors said Kaczynski's handwritten diary contained phrases such as "I mailed that bomb" or "I sent that bomb."

According to news reports, investigators also found at the cabin bomb components, an original copy of the Unabomber's rambling, 35,000-word anti-technology manifesto sent to newspapers in 1995 and a typewriter used to type it.
Federal prosecutors said they acted in good faith and that the search warrant was properly obtained. They argued that they had to act fast because the Unabomber was dangerous.
Prosecutor J. Douglas Wilson said the defence arguments were no more than "frivolous criticisms."
Judge Burrell did not rule Friday on the defence motion to suppress evidence seized from the cabin, but said he would review court filings and issue a written decision later.
"I will rule as soon as I can," Burrell said. "It will take some time."
Kaczynski made a rare appearance in court for the hearing in Sacramento. He wore a brown jacket, black slacks, and a white open-collared shirt.
He appeared to be following the arguments closely during the hearing, which lasted more than two hours. When court was adjourned, he smiled and shook hands with his lawyers.
